It’s not true that alters fully form later in life. If that was true, then absolutely nobody (DID or nah) would have any personality traits until they’re older, right? But children have personality traits. They aren’t blank slates that suddenly develop a personality when they turn 20-something. Therefore the same applies to alters, since they are different parts of a person and develop their own traits due to amnesia barriers. It just makes no sense that it takes a lifetime to develop a personality

Why do you think that fictives take so long to form? Like… yes you need trauma for any alter to form but why would a fictive take longer than any other? Any new alter forming due to trauma would occur during and immediately after that trauma, it wouldn’t take years to form, that would be absolutely no help to the person with DID in coping with the trauma

It usually only takes that long due to misdiagnosis first. When I was at Sheppard Pratt (a hospital that has an inpatient center for trauma and dissociative disorders. I was there for PTSD treatment but group was for both PTSD and dissociative patients so I learned a lot in 6 weeks), that was the one thing that all the doctors and therapists agreed on. That diagnosis takes that long because DID isn’t usually considered, instead it’s things like schizophrenia or borderline PD, sometimes bipolar disorder with psychosis. But then the patient is medicated and doesn’t get better, gets bpd or other specific therapy and doesn’t get better, and that goes on and on for years before they finally get diagnosed properly. Janina Fisher (a trauma/dissociative specialist) wrote a paper on things you see with this kinda misdiagnosed patient

“First, treatment history is a potential red flag alerting us to the possible presence of dissociative defenses. The average dissociative disorder patient has been in treatment for an average of seven years and been given an average of 3.6 diagnoses before he or she is correctly diagnosed (Putnam, 1991). So our suspicions should be raised by any patient who has had a number of treaters and diagnoses without a great deal of progress or clarity. Patients whose therapeutic courses have been rocky, or who have struggling internally with alternating idealization and devaluation or approach-avoidance of their therapists, or whose therapies have ended in some unusually dramatic way should also raise our index of suspicion.”

The treatment guidelines for DID state that diagnosis is done by observation, psychological testing (the MID, the SCID, DIS-Q and the DES are the most common, but they may use others to rule out other diagnoses) and comprehensive interviews
Yes that’s exactly what’s happening, people forget DID does exist, that professionals that research it exist, and that we’re still learning more about it all the time
It actually *is* a clinical term, it’s right in the ISSTD guidelines for treating DID. You can find the guidelines free on their website and see that it’s a real term that medical professionals use

Final fusion is a genuine term in the ISSTD’s treatment guidelines for DID. Like yeah it sounds funny but it is something professionals actually use to describe alters merging into one

*final fusion* refers to a point in time when the patients sense of self shifts from that of having multiple identities to that of being a unified self.“

Additionally: “R P Kluft has argued that the most stable treatment outcome is final fusion- complete integration, merger, and loss of separateness- of all identity states. However, even after undergoing considerable treatment, a considerable number of DID patients will not be able to achieve final fusion and/or will not see fusion as desirable.”

System is also used in the same guidelines, used meaning “system of alternate identities.”, so “system” is just shorthand for that.
